articles.title: Experts in Canada are testing doorbell cameras' for Polar bears, called Bear-vision, they combine radar and cameras to …
articles.summary: Researchers are testing Bear-vision cameras to warn communities in Canada about approaching polar bears.
articles.body: Researchers are testing Bear-vision cameras to warn communities in Canada about approaching polar bears. Conservation charity Polar Bears International is developing Bear-vision, a warning system built on security camera technology that can be paired with shorter-range radar. Its first deployment is planned at Churchill’s waste facility this autumn to help monitor bears and reduce surprise encounters, the organisation’ noted in a blog post.The camera is intended to offer a more affordable, easy-to-use alternative to wide-area radar systems. Researchers will use data gathered at the site to train it to recognise polar bears and send notifications when they appear. The project comes as bears gather along Hudson Bay, waiting for sea ice to return so they can hunt seals, while communities work to keep people and wildlife safely apart.How will Bear-vision workBear-vision builds on the organisation’s earlier Bear-dar detection work. While Bear-dar monitors wider areas using radar, the new system uses smart security camera technology and can incorporate shorter-range radar.​Polar Bears International compares the intended function to a doorbell camera that alerts residents when a polar bear is outside. The Churchill deployment will help researchers gather the information needed to train the notification system.Why is Churchill’s waste facility the first locationChurchill began working with Polar Bears International to keep bears out of its dump after a fire destroyed its waste facilities. Garbage can attract bears looking for food, creating risks for both the animals and people nearby.The response includes new electric fences, Bear-dar and Bear-vision monitoring, and a visit by a Churchill delegation to a waste management facility in Greenland. The camera trial is part of a broader effort to manage the site, not replace physical barriers or other measures.Why are bears spending longer near communitiesPolar Bears International says climate-driven sea ice loss leaves bears waiting on land about a month longer than their grandparents did. The ice-free period around Hudson Bay now lasts three to four weeks longer than in the 1980s, placing additional strain on their stored fat reserves.The organisation says these longer periods ashore make coexistence measures increasingly important. Its Polar Bear Week, running November 1–7, coincides with the seasonal gathering near Churchill.What other tools are researchers testingPolar Bears International and Brigham Young University are also working with Churchill’s Polar Bear Alert Program to test drones as an affordable, non-lethal way to move bears away from communities. That separate deterrent project includes ultrasonic sound, conductive materials and a new odour-based bear spray formula.​“It’s not easy to live with large predators as your neighbours, so we’re investing in coexistence approaches, especially as we see climate change causing more human-bear encounters. By developing and field-testing innovative, non-lethal deterrents like drones and detection tech like Bear-vision, we’re hoping to expand the variety of safe, effective, and affordable coexistence tools available to communities,” said Geoff York, Polar Bears International’s vice president of science and policy.​​You use AI every day. articles.title: 'He's done a fantastic job': Trump backs Hegseth amid growing calls for his removal
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has defended secretary of war Pete Hegseth amid calls for his resignation and impeachment, praising his work and backing the US
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has defended secretary of war Pete Hegseth amid calls for his resignation and impeachment, praising his work and backing the US military operations in Iran and Venezuela.When asked whether he was considering changes to his administration, particularly at the Pentagon, Trump dismissed criticism of Hegseth and said the defence chief had performed "a fantastic job"."United States Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, has done a fantastic job. Now, it's got some interesting things. You know, we had more generals than we did in World War II. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it. And many of those people were woke. I don't like a woke general, and so he probably has opposition. I think he's done a fantastic job," Trump said.The president also sought to defend his administration's military record, citing operations involving Venezuela and Iran as evidence of the Pentagon's performance. He claimed the operation in Venezuela was completed in 48 minutes without any American fatalities, describing it as one of the greatest attacks witnessed.He also claimed Iran could take 25 to 30 years to recover from the military campaign, while keeping open the possibility of further strikes.The pressure on Hegseth comes in the aftermath of the November 3 midterm elections, in which Republican losses are expected to strengthen Democratic oversight of the Trump administration.Hegseth faces impeachment pressureTrump's public endorsement comes as Hegseth faces growing scrutiny from lawmakers over the administration's handling of the Iran conflict, with members of Congress calling for his removal.Republican Congressman Thomas Massie said on November 4 that he would not reintroduce impeachment articles against Hegseth if the Pentagon chief resigned."There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said in a post on X, according to CNN.Democratic Congressman Jason Crow has also demanded Hegseth's removal, alleging that his leadership has put American military personnel at greater risk.Meanwhile, Hegseth posted a video on X Thursday defending the war against Iran.Hegseth described the Iran war as a “courageous and historic effort” that he said would “ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” He dismissed the impeachment articles against him as a “sham,” accusing political opponents of trying to destroy their rivals.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2026, 20 scientists, artists and writers received $800,000 each through the MacArthur 'genius' grants; here is what their work aims to change
articles.summary: The MacArthur Foundation has named 20 fellows whose work spans climate science, history, philosophy, chemistry, poetry, dance and jazz.
articles.body: The MacArthur Foundation has named 20 fellows whose work spans climate science, history, philosophy, chemistry, poetry, dance and jazz. The prize rewards people rather than projects, and nobody can apply for it. Nominations feed a selection process lasting years, and many recipients say they were stunned by the news. The recognition often opens further doors. Reading the full class together shows recurring concerns: damage to the climate and the environment, the memory of violence and injustice, hidden or erased communities, and technology that could make medicine, farming and materials safer and more efficient.Researchers aim to bring communities into clean energy, forecast polar ice and predict harvestsAccording to The Associated Press, Holly Jean Buck, a sociologist at the University at Buffalo, studies the part local communities play in limiting climate change and moving towards clean energy. Marika Holland, a climate scientist based in Boulder, Colorado, helps predict changes in ice cover and works out how polar climate change affects marine ecosystems.Kaiyu Guan, an environmental scientist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, uses data and machine learning to help farmers predict and optimise their crop yields.Scholars revisit history to explain racial wealth gaps, Indigenous nationhood and federal powerEllora Derenoncourt, a labour economist at Princeton University, investigates where racial wealth disparities in the United States came from and which policies could narrow the gap. Her Princeton colleague Elizabeth Ellis, a historian, is correcting the colonial record to highlight the different ideas of nationhood held by Indigenous tribes and the strategies Native Americans used to resist European settlement.Ariel Ron, a historian at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, examines how agriculture in the northern states influenced economic growth and the expansion of federal power in nineteenth-century America.Memory, forgiveness and loss: A philosopher, a forensic anthropologist, a novelist and a poetFelipe De Brigard, a philosopher at Duke University, applies cognitive science to the link between memory and forgiveness, including among victims of political violence in his home country of Colombia. Kate Spradley, a forensic anthropologist at Texas State University, works to identify migrants who died along the Texas-Mexico border and to repatriate their remains. Her Operation Identification initiative also tackles the complications that make this work so difficult.Maaza Mengiste, a fiction writer at Wesleyan University, uses historically informed novels to show the human cost of political conflict. Layli Long Soldier, a poet in Santa Fe, reworks historical texts to underline the erasure of Native Americans and pairs her writing with visual art.Dance, sound, murals and jazz, artists reimagine whose stories are told and how they are heardTrajal Harrell, a choreographer and dancer based in Zurich, merges dance traditions into an imagined archive that dissolves the barriers between styles. Christine Sun Kim, an artist in Berlin, conveys the experiences of deaf people and finds new ways to understand sound through drawings, large-scale murals, video and interactive works.Rodney McMillian, an artist at the University of California, Los Angeles, moves between sculpture, painting, video and performance to explore how history and socioeconomic conditions shape belonging in the American South. Chip Thomas, a public artist in Flagstaff, Arizona, turns neglected spaces, mostly in the Navajo Nation, into public works rooted in community history.Vincent Valdez, who divides his time between Houston and San Antonio, paints historical and contemporary scenes that reflect Latino experiences in the United States. Immanuel Wilkins, a New York alto saxophonist and composer, writes music that often reflects historical narratives of injustice. Bryan Washington, a fiction writer in Tokyo, captures modern relationships in novels including “Memorial” and “Palaver”.Chemistry, physics and nanotechnology: Safer reactions, new materials and better disease treatmentsSong Lin, an organic chemist at Stanford University, develops methods that open routes to safer and more sustainable synthetic organic reactions. Vincenzo Vitelli, a physicist at the University of Chicago, builds theoretical frameworks to describe how matter and materials with unusual properties will behave.Liangfang Zhang, a chemical engineer and bioengineer at the University of California, San Diego, is creating new nanotechnologies to treat and prevent infectious diseases, cancers and immunological disorders.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, Denzel Washington helped lead a $5 million effort to rescue playwright August Wilson's deteriorating childhood home in Pittsburgh; it reopened in 2022 as a 6,000-square-foot arts and community centre
articles.summary: Some houses preserve memories, while others hold the beginnings of stories that eventually shape generations.
articles.body: Some houses preserve memories, while others hold the beginnings of stories that eventually shape generations. In Pittsburgh's historic Hill District, a modest childhood home has become a lasting tribute to one of America's most celebrated playwrights, August Wilson. Once deteriorating and at risk of being lost, the property where Wilson spent his formative years has been transformed into a 6,000-square-foot arts and community centre. The restoration, supported by a fundraising campaign led by Hollywood actor Denzel Washington, has given the building a renewed purpose while preserving the surroundings that influenced Wilson's celebrated body of work. Scroll down to read the details.A childhood home saved from decayAccording to Architectural Digest, Washington spearheaded a $5 million fundraising initiative in September 2018 to support the restoration of Wilson's childhood home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The Oscar-winning actor, who directed and starred in the 2016 film adaptation of Wilson's play Fences, was among the prominent supporters who helped mobilise resources for the project.Other contributors included Oprah Winfrey, Tyler Perry, Shonda Rhimes, Spike Lee and Samuel L. Jackson, with Winfrey and Perry each contributing $1 million.Wilson, born Frederick August Kittel Jr., lived in the Bedford Avenue property with his mother, Daisy, and five siblings from 1945 to 1958. The neighbourhood, known as the Hill District, would later become an important influence on his writing, providing the cultural and social backdrop for much of his work, the Architectural Digest report adds.However, by the early 2000s, the building had fallen into disrepair. According to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, Wilson's nephew, Paul Ellis, purchased the property shortly before the playwright's death in 2005, hoping to preserve it. Together with architect Rob Pfaffmann, he established the nonprofit Daisy Wilson Artist Community to oversee its restoration.From a deteriorating building to a cultural destinationThe preservation process involved several years of planning and structural work. The property received Pittsburgh historic landmark status in 2008, followed by emergency stabilisation efforts between 2010 and 2016. It was also added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2013.The $5 million fundraising campaign launched in 2018 enabled the larger restoration to move forward. Although the project was initially expected to finish in 2020, the pandemic caused delays. The restored property eventually reopened in August 2022.The 6,000-square-foot complex brings together the original 1840s house, an upstairs expansion dating to the 1880s and a contemporary addition. The newer section incorporates elevators, ensuring accessibility throughout the building while allowing its historic architectural elements to remain visible.Preserving Wilson's legacy through the artsRather than functioning solely as a conventional museum, August Wilson House was designed as an active cultural and community space. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that Wilson had wanted his childhood home to remain useful, particularly as a place that could support artists and creative expression.The centre includes four studios for artistic programmes, workshops, reading sessions and discussions. Two indoor galleries will showcase rotating exhibitions, while a rooftop terrace provides space for live performances overlooking Pittsburgh's skyline.Outside, a landscaped garden and outdoor theatre offer opportunities for productions of Wilson's celebrated American Century Cycle, a collection of ten plays exploring African-American experiences across different decades of the 20th century.Inside the rooms where the playwright grew upOne of the most significant sections of the restoration is the preserved upstairs apartment where Wilson spent his childhood. The living room, kitchen, and bedrooms have been meticulously restored to match the family's original surroundings.Details include replica wallpaper based on recollections from Wilson's sister, vintage kitchen appliances and photographic displays featuring images of the Hill District. Restoration workers also uncovered personal artefacts, including shoes concealed inside the walls, believed to have been placed there for good luck.The project concludes by honoring the playwright and his neighborhood. With its combination of preserved domestic spaces, contemporary architecture and creative facilities, August Wilson House offers visitors an opportunity to experience the roots of his storytelling while giving future generations of artists a place to develop their own voices.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia, Facebook, and Pittsburgh Post-GazetteYou use AI every day. articles.title: In 1944, Canadian Captain W. E. Duggan Gray lost his engraved silver flask in France; fellow soldier James McCorriston kept it and returned it nearly 48 years later
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of how a silver flask, lost by Canadian Captain W.E. Duggan Gray in 1944 during WWII, was returned 48 years later by fellow soldier James McCorriston, showcasing the enduring power of memories and connections forged in battle.
articles.body: Some lost things remain lost forever. Others show up when least expected. According to the Royal Canadian Artillery Museum, an engraved silver flask belonging to Canadian captain W.E. Duggan Gray was lost in France in 1944. It ended up with another soldier, James McCorriston, who kept it safe for decades. Finally, in 1992, he returned it, nearly 48 years after it disappeared.A young officer on Juno BeachGray landed on Juno Beach on D-Day, June 6, 1944. He was serving with the 3rd Anti-Tank Regiment, a unit in the 3rd Canadian Division. A Veterans Affairs Canada backgrounder says there were approximately 14,000 Canadians who landed at Juno Beach on June 6, 1944, where they were met with intense enemy fire. The Germans had heavily fortified the coastline with machine guns, mines, and barbed wire. A separate Veterans Affairs Canada web page on the Bény-sur-Mer Canadian War Cemetery states that the 3rd Division and the 2nd Armoured Brigade formed the main Canadian ground force for that day. Gray’s regiment paid dearly for the war. The museum notes one of his batteries had lost 50 percent over 3 days.A wound and a terrible mix-up In 1944, Gray was still fighting in France when a German mortar hit his leg. British soldiers found him and took him to a hospital. Then things went wrong. His unit thought he was dead and sent a telegram to his family saying so. His parents were grief-stricken. The unit corrected the mistake shortly after they found out Gray was alive and recovering. In a 1992 newspaper article, Gray described himself back in 1944 as “young, stupid, and very fatalistic.” He added that he laughed about the mix-up afterwards.How the flask went missingThere was yet another consequence of the false news. Before anyone realised that Gray was alive, his regiment had sent his kit to the divisional headquarters to get rid of it. The kit had his silver flask with the inscription “D.Gray” on it, and it was full of military rum. Once Gray was discovered alive, his regiment went back for his belongings. By that time, however, the rum and the flask had disappeared. The loss was minor compared to the war around it. Gray didn't know that McCorriston, another Canadian soldier, was carrying the flask through the rest of the war.The search that ended at a dinnerMcCorriston kept the flask for decades after the war. With the assistance of the War Graves Commission and Legion Magazine, he traced its owner in 1991. He returned it to Gray in 1992 at the reunion dinner of the 3rd Anti-Tank Regiment. The Vernon Daily News published a story on January 18, 1992, with a headline saying the flask was back after 47 years. McCorriston said that a girl had given him the flask, while Gray believed McCorriston had helped himself to the rum.Why a small object still matters Gray was mentioned twice in dispatches by the Canadian military for service in France and Belgium. Later, he passed his wartime keepsakes to his son. In 2008, his son, Nairne Gray, of Vancouver, donated them to the museum. The collection included the flask, a Second World War helmet, a framed set of medals, discharge papers and one newspaper article. The family donated the items to the museum to keep the legacy of their father, the museum said. A flask is just metal, but this one held an entire story of a wound, a fake death notice and a very long wait. The story shows that behind every great date in history are real people, and little things like this one help keep their stories alive.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
